file: papers/pdf/Wareham et al - 2022 - Systematizing Serendipity for Big Science Infrastructures.pdf
about: The paper studies ATTRACT, an EU program funding 170 proof-of-concept projects, to identify how big-science researchers serendipitously find alternative commercial applications of their technologies (combining technologies, applying to another field, using AI/ML) and which antecedents and program features enable these modes.

candidates.label: Unanticipated beneficial discovery
candidates.definition: Serendipity is the unanticipated discovery of something beneficial, specifically technologies finding applications outside their original intended use.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes a technology or finding turning out to be useful for something it was not originally meant for, and this was not anticipated.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The use was the planned target from the outset (pseudo-serendipity) or is a routine extension of existing research.

candidates.label: Accident plus sagacity
candidates.definition: Serendipity combines accident with sagacity (a prepared mind, perception and sound judgment); in entrepreneurship, directed search, favourable accidents and prior knowledge. It is a capability requiring focused attention, not mere luck.
candidates.applies_when: Account shows a chance event paired with the person's perception, judgment or prior knowledge that let them recognize its value.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person attributes the outcome purely to luck with no role for their own attention or knowledge.

candidates.label: Pseudo-serendipity vs serendipity
candidates.definition: de Rond distinguishes pseudo-serendipity, where the solution was intended in the first place, from serendipity proper, where the solution is completely unanticipated or accidental.
candidates.applies_when: Account indicates whether the person was looking for the solution they found (pseudo) or found something wholly unanticipated (serendipity).

candidates.label: Exaptation: franklins and miltons
candidates.definition: Exaptation is the emergence of unanticipated functionalities; franklins are existing structures co-opted for an unintended use, miltons are discoveries without a currently known function that may later be co-opted.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes repurposing an existing tool/technology for a new role (franklin) or holding a discovery with no known use that later finds one (milton).

candidates.label: Yaqub's four archetypes
candidates.definition: Walpolian (targeted search yields a solution to a different problem), Mertonian (targeted problem solved via unexpected route), Bushian (untargeted exploration solves a known problem), Stephanian (untargeted research yields an unsought solution with later application).
candidates.applies_when: Account allows classification by whether the inquiry was targeted and whether the solution addressed the original, a different, or a future problem.

candidates.label: Combining different technologies
candidates.definition: Technologies or knowledge from different (adjacent or distant) domains are combined, integrated or assembled to produce a new application, from assembling off-the-shelf components to merging disjoint disciplines.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes creating a new application by merging technologies or knowledge from different fields or assembling existing components.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: A single technology is simply moved into a new field without combination (applying to another field), or improved within its own domain.

candidates.label: Applying technology to another field
candidates.definition: Technology or knowledge from one domain is used in a new research domain or application area, exposing it to a field where new use cases emerge; closest to classic notions of finding new uses for existing things.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes taking an existing technology into a field it had not been used in to find a new use.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The technology is extended within its original domain (baseline extension).

candidates.label: Using AI or machine learning
candidates.definition: Computational advances in AI/ML are used to extend or find new uses for existing technologies, e.g., extracting patterns from sensor data; in the sample mostly to improve efficacy rather than discover new applications.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes applying AI/ML to existing technology or data to create new capability or use.

candidates.label: Extending extant research
candidates.definition: Improving existing technologies to be more effective or efficient within the same domain is normal research advancement, not serendipity.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes making a technology more powerful/efficient or operable in harsher conditions while staying in the same application area.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The technology is moved to a new field or combined with others for a new application.

candidates.label: Methodical problem-solving
candidates.definition: Some projects started from identifying a problem and methodically working to resolve it, contrasting with burst-like surprise insight.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes the venture idea originating from a deliberately identified need pursued through systematic effort.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The idea arose from a surprise insight or anomaly.

candidates.label: Surprise personal insight
candidates.definition: Consistent with traditional notions, some ideas originated from a surprise personal insight (21% of projects).
candidates.applies_when: Account describes a sudden unexpected realization as the origin of the idea.

candidates.label: Anomalies in research
candidates.definition: Ideas came from anomalies or unclear results in ongoing or previous research that needed revisiting.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes an unexpected or unclear result prompting the idea for a new application.

candidates.label: Environmental cue in process model
candidates.definition: In McCay-Peet and Toms' process, a trigger (environmental cue sparking interest) is connected to prior knowledge, followed up to a valuable outcome, with surprise noticed afterwards.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes a cue that caught attention, was linked to the person's experience, and was then followed up.

candidates.label: Ideas from day-to-day work
candidates.definition: Scientists and engineers develop many ideas about novel applications in their daily work, mostly as extensions of their research; most had the idea before the funding call.
candidates.applies_when: Account traces the venture idea to the person's routine work and research activity before any formal program.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The idea was sparked by an external call or program (activated ideas).

candidates.label: Prior relationships with partners
candidates.definition: Most teams knew their partners and had collaborated before; pre-existing relationships between infrastructures and industrial suppliers were leveraged.
candidates.applies_when: Account mentions pre-existing collaborators or supplier ties forming the basis of the venture team.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Partners met for the first time through the program.

candidates.label: De-risked deep technology
candidates.definition: Technologies from big-science infrastructures are already developed and operated at scale, making them de-risked, yet they are specialized, interdependent enabling technologies far from markets whose alternate applications are less apparent.
candidates.applies_when: Account draws on sophisticated pre-existing infrastructure technology as the basis for a new application, or notes difficulty seeing its applications.

candidates.label: Organizational enablers of serendipity
candidates.definition: Prior literature lists conditions conducive to serendipity: boundary spanning, mindfulness, social networks, teamwork, free space for creativity, play with ideas, and structures like databases, fairs and workshops.
candidates.applies_when: Account mentions such settings or practices as enabling the unexpected discovery.

candidates.label: Individual serendipity strategies
candidates.definition: Actionable strategies: varying routines, being observant, making mental space, relaxing boundaries, drawing on experience, seeking patterns, seizing opportunities; examining deviations, tolerating errors, leveraging networks.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes the person deliberately doing such things that made a lucky find more likely.

candidates.label: Social interactions and networks
candidates.definition: Social relations with a wide range of actors increase chances of unexpected encounters; the program required multi-organization collaboration to promote serendipitous interactions.
candidates.applies_when: Account credits interactions with diverse partners or networks for the idea or its development.

candidates.label: Geographic proximity
candidates.definition: Projects involving more countries were less likely to combine technologies or apply them to another field, likely due to coordination costs; colocation enables close iteration.
candidates.applies_when: Account notes that nearby partners eased (or distant ones hindered) combining or transferring technologies.

candidates.label: Perceived unfundability
candidates.definition: Teams pursuing combination or cross-field application often had not sought funding before, apparently believing such serendipitous ideas would not be fundable; without dedicated instruments they might cease to exist.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes holding back from seeking funding because the unconventional idea seemed unlikely to be funded.

candidates.label: Cross-field applicable technology
candidates.definition: Data acquisition and computing techniques are unbound to specific artifacts, increasing cross-field applicability and positively relating to all modes.
candidates.applies_when: Account involves generic data/computing technology that was easily transferred to new uses.

candidates.label: Science-business tensions
candidates.definition: Cultures antagonistic to commercialization, long scientific timescales versus short venture capital horizons, and deep-tech capital needs hinder pursuing alternate applications.
candidates.applies_when: Account mentions cultural reluctance to commercialize, mismatch of timelines, or investor impatience as obstacles.

candidates.label: Funding advances existing ideas
candidates.definition: The program's main value was not sparking new ideas but providing resources, timely support and industrial brokering to move pre-existing ideas toward proof of concept; a few ideas were 'activated' by the call.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes external funding or programs enabling development of an already-held idea, or a call prompting an idea.

candidates.label: Brokering industrial partners
candidates.definition: Relationships with industrial partners providing complementary skills for later product development and commercialization were most important for taking technologies outside their original domain.
candidates.applies_when: Account highlights industry partners brokered or brought in to help commercialize the new application.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Relationships among scientists for idea generation.

candidates.label: Funding enables new research lines
candidates.definition: Funding allowed teams to pursue lines they otherwise would not, such as integrating AI, a mode teams had the luxury of following only due to funding.
candidates.applies_when: Account says resources allowed exploration of an unplanned direction.

candidates.label: Protracted process not flash insight
candidates.definition: Serendipity here departs from a romanticized flash-insight ideal and resembles a protracted, partially controlled process of systematic exploration under high uncertainty.
candidates.applies_when: Account narrates the discovery as a long, effortful exploration across options rather than a single eureka moment.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Account narrates a sudden surprise insight.

candidates.label: Ex post characterization
candidates.definition: Typologies of serendipity mostly characterize unexpected outcomes after they occur, with researchers narrating in proposals how they came up with new applications.
candidates.applies_when: Account retrospectively frames how an unexpected application came about.
